claims.statement: Compare a supplied initial configuration with a fixed number of random configurations, then perform randomized first-acceptable one-exchange local search. Exclude moves that change only a currently inactive conditional parameter. Repeatedly perturb the current search configuration by a fixed number of random neighborhood moves, apply the local-search routine, and accept the resulting configuration when the chosen comparison procedure judges it at least as good. Independently restart the search configuration at random with a specified probability. Maintain an overall incumbent and return it at termination. The framework deliberately leaves comparison and objective estimation to an instantiation such as BasicILS or FocusedILS.

claims.statement: Within the ParamILS search framework, compare configurations using cached target-algorithm runs on a common ordered instance/seed sequence. A configuration dominates another when it has at least as many runs and its estimated cost over the other’s full prefix is no greater. Begin a comparison by extending the shorter prefix by one run, or both when their lengths are equal; continue extending until either configuration dominates. Procedure3 increments its global bonus counter once per comparison and again when the initial run counts tie. When the first configuration dominates, add the accumulated number of bonus evaluations to it and reset the counter; otherwise return the unsuccessful comparison without that reset. Keep an incumbent while the search continues.

entries.name: Random Online Aggressive Racing
entries.definition: An algorithm-configuration procedure that proposes uniformly random parameter settings and compares each challenger with an incumbent through adaptive evaluations on shared problem instances and random seeds, without fitting a predictive performance model.
entries.identity_notes: The 2011 source expands ROAR as Random Online Adaptive Racing in its introduction and Random Online Aggressive Racing in Section3. Both wordings here refer to that source’s same method. It shares SMAC’s intensification procedure but omits SMAC’s random-forest surrogate and acquisition-guided proposals. It differs from fixed-evaluation random search and significance-based elimination in F-Race. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 265 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 20 lines in the worktree and 25 in main. These were prior candidate leads, source references, neighboring-method mentions and five unrelated ROAR namespace entries in ignored dependencies, not existing records for these identities. Seven exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Aggressive racing in this source makes empirical decisions without waiting for a statistical significance threshold. An early rejection can discard a configuration with better expected performance; no family-wise error control or finite-budget optimum is claimed.

The shared intensification routine caps incumbent runs at maxR=2000. Its time-budget early-exit guard requires i>=2, but ROAR supplies one challenger per call, so the proposal loop ends after that one challenger; the guard is not a mandatory two-challenger minimum for ROAR. The paper’s asymptotic discussion assumes consistent estimation and unbounded evaluation growth in a finite configuration space, which are not automatic properties of the capped practical routine.

The original procedure lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Uniform configuration proposals do not mean equal allocation of evaluations to every configuration. No implementation or benchmark outcome was reproduced.

claims.statement: Initialize by evaluating the default configuration or a random setting when a default is unavailable. Supply uniformly random configurations to the intensification routine; the nominal model is constant and unused for proposing them. Add an incumbent evaluation, subject to the maximum-run cap, on an instance with the fewest incumbent runs and a random seed. Evaluate a challenger on a subset of the incumbent’s instance/seed pairs and compare their empirical costs on exactly those pairs. Reject a worse challenger; otherwise enlarge its tested subset in doubling batches until it has covered the incumbent’s available runs, then replace the incumbent when the challenger remains at least as good. Continue proposing random challengers within the configuration budget.

entries.name: F-Race
entries.definition: A statistical racing method for configuring metaheuristics that evaluates a finite candidate set on shared problem-instance blocks and eliminates candidates judged worse through a Friedman rank test followed by comparisons with the best-ranked candidate.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers the original 2002 F-Race method. It uses a fixed starting candidate pool and nested survivor sets, not iterative resampling of configurations as in later iterated racing methods. It differs from ROAR’s challenger-incumbent heuristic comparisons, fixed-fraction successive halving and a standalone Friedman test without sequential resource allocation. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 265 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 20 lines in the worktree and 25 in main. These were prior candidate leads, source references, neighboring-method mentions and five unrelated ROAR namespace entries in ignored dependencies, not existing records for these identities. Seven exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The method assumes independent instance blocks and appropriate within-block comparability. The aggregate test uses an approximate chi-square reference distribution, followed by the paper’s Student-t-based pairwise rule. No implementation-level small-sample correction or sequential family-wise error guarantee was verified.

Rank comparisons discard cost magnitudes. Better rank sums need not identify the lowest arithmetic mean cost, so the method is not asserted to certify the minimizer of the expected-cost objective stated in Section2. Repeated significance decisions and early elimination do not ensure that the best configuration survives.

A finite initial candidate pool limits what can be selected, and the time budget can expire with multiple survivors. The inspected method does not establish a unique returned configuration in every such case. No general superiority over parametric racing methods or replicated TSP result is claimed.

claims.statement: Start with a finite set of candidate configurations and draw a sequence of training instances independently from the selected instance distribution. At each racing step, evaluate every surviving candidate on the same new instance and append its observed solution cost. Rank surviving candidates by cost within each accumulated instance block, using average ranks for ties. Apply the paper’s Friedman aggregate rank statistic to the accumulated blocks. If its null is not rejected, retain all survivors; if rejected, compare each candidate with the best-ranked one using the stated post-hoc rank-difference test and discard candidates found worse. Repeat with the reduced candidate set until one remains or the prescribed total computation budget stops further evaluation.

native_neighbors.name: Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential algorithm-configuration procedure that uses random-forest performance models to propose parameter settings and compares candidate settings with an incumbent through adaptive evaluations on shared problem instances and random seeds.

claims.statement: Initialize with an evaluation of the default configuration, or a random setting when no default is available. Fit a random-forest surrogate using configuration values and, when available, training-instance features. Aggregate each tree’s predictions over instances according to the chosen cost metric, then derive predictive moments across trees. For runtime optimization the paper uses log-transformed responses while preserving the original aggregation objective through inverse transformation at leaves. Rank proposals by expected improvement, using its log-cost formulation, and search for promising settings with multistart one-coordinate local changes plus randomly sampled acquisition candidates. Interleave guided proposals with uniformly sampled configurations. The intensification routine compares a challenger and incumbent on shared instance/seed evaluations, enlarges the challenger’s evaluated subset in doubling batches, rejects it when its empirical cost is worse, and replaces the incumbent when the challenger has matched the available evaluation set and is at least as good. Repeat model fitting and configuration comparisons within the overall configuration budget.

evidence.locator: Sections2–4.3, PDF pp.3–9, especially Framework1, Procedure2 and Equation1; original scope and limitations in Sections1 and6, PDF pp.1–3 and14

aio_mappings.rationale: The original SMAC algorithm uses a random-forest regression surrogate as a component. The full proposal-and-comparison procedure is neither identical to that ensemble model nor a subclass of it; this is a component-based conceptual relation.

limitations: The original method explicitly lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Its adaptive allocation of additional evaluations must not be equated with the censored-runtime handling or other features of later SMAC releases.

Surrogate uncertainty and early empirical comparisons do not certify an optimal configuration or generalization to unseen instance distributions. The paper’s asymptotic argument assumes a finite configuration space, consistent cost estimates and unbounded evaluation growth; the displayed experimental procedure caps incumbent evaluations with maxR=2000. These conditions are not an unconditional guarantee for the capped implementation or continuous spaces.

Instance features are optional; the result is a single configuration and does not require test-instance feature computation. The reviewed source is an author-hosted manuscript, not a claim that its 15 PDF pages match the publisher’s page layout. No benchmark result or executable implementation was reproduced.

native_neighbors.name: Hyperband
native_neighbors.definition: A hyperparameter resource-allocation algorithm that runs successive-halving brackets with different initial configuration counts and starting budgets, balancing broad early screening against more conservative evaluation.

claims.statement: Choose a maximum per-configuration resource R and reduction factor eta. In the finite-horizon Algorithm1, set s_max=floor(log_eta(R)) and B=(s_max+1)*R. For each bracket s from s_max down to zero, start with n=ceil((B/R)*eta^s/(s+1)) configurations and r=R*eta^(−s) resource units. Evaluate current candidates at geometrically increasing resource levels and retain the best approximately 1/eta fraction after each comparison. The s=0 bracket evaluates its candidates directly at R. Algorithm1 returns the configuration with the smallest intermediate loss observed, rather than specifying selection only among maximum-budget evaluations. Brackets address uncertainty about how many configurations to start and how long to evaluate before elimination. Resources can denote iterations, time, data or features; actual computational cost and whether work can be resumed depend on that choice.

native_neighbors.name: Successive Halving
native_neighbors.definition: A staged best-candidate selection algorithm that divides a resource budget across elimination rounds, evaluates surviving candidates with comparable within-round effort, removes approximately the poorer-performing half, and allocates more effort per remaining candidate in later rounds.

claims.statement: Start with a finite candidate set and a total allocation budget, divide effort across elimination rounds, evaluate the current survivors, retain their better-performing subset, and repeat with fewer candidates and more effort per survivor. The original stochastic Sequential Halving allocates floor(T/(|S|*ceil(log2(n)))) samples per surviving arm in a round, ranks stage empirical reward averages, and keeps ceil(|S|/2) arms with the highest averages. The non-stochastic hyperparameter formulation instead allocates additional training pulls and compares current validation losses at cumulative training progress; it minimizes these losses rather than averaging raw observations as if they were i.i.d. rewards. Its analysis assumes fixed loss sequences with limits but does not require the convergence envelopes as inputs. Randomly sampled or prespecified configurations can supply the finite cohort. Resume within a candidate’s own training trajectory; the mechanism does not copy weights between candidates.

native_neighbors.name: Asynchronous Successive Halving
native_neighbors.definition: An asynchronous resource-allocation algorithm that promotes promising completed hyperparameter trials through increasing resource levels as workers become available and starts new trials when no eligible promotion is available, without waiting for an entire evaluation stage to finish.

claims.statement: Choose minimum and maximum resources r and R, a reduction factor eta, and starting-level offset s. Resource at rung k is r*eta^(s+k). Dispatch work to free workers and record completed rung losses. In the author dissertation’s Algorithm 3, scan promotable rungs from the highest eligible level downward, stopping below the maximum-resource rung. At each level, consider the currently best approximately 1/eta fraction of completed configurations and select an eligible one that has not already been promoted. If the entire scan yields none, sample a new configuration for the base rung. Thus the starting cohort can grow and promotions do not wait for every job at a rung. Promoted configurations may later fall outside the hindsight top fraction as additional results arrive. Checkpointing can reuse a trial’s previous training; it is distinct from copying weights between different configurations. The maximum resource limits promotion depth in this bounded version.
